concept.name: Contract multiplier
concept.definition: The fixed dollar amount per unit of quoted price (or per index point) set by the exchange in the contract specification, which converts a quoted price into the total monetary value of one contract; for equity options the standardized multiplier is typically 100 shares per contract.
concept.intuition: Quotes come in points, but money moves in dollars — the multiplier is the exchange-fixed exchange rate between the two.
concept.mechanics: Contract dollar value = quoted price x contract multiplier (for unit-quoted contracts, price x contract size plays the same role). A one-point price move changes the position value by exactly one multiplier unit, which is also how tick value is derived (tick size x multiplier).
concept.formula: Contract value = P x M, where P = quoted futures price (or index level) and M = contract multiplier ($ per point); equity option premium in dollars = quoted premium x 100 (shares per contract).
concept.failure_modes: Using the wrong multiplier (e.g., confusing standard, mini, or micro variants of the same product) scales P&L, margin, and hedge ratios incorrectly — a 10x or 50x error in position sizing.
concept.misconceptions: The multiplier is not chosen by the trader and is not universal: it is fixed per contract by the exchange and differs across products (e.g., $50 per point for E-mini S&P 500 vs $5 for the Micro E-mini).
concept.example: A U.S. listed equity call quoted at $2.50 represents $250 per contract because standardized equity options use a 100-share multiplier; likewise an index future quoted at 5,000 with a $50 multiplier controls $250,000 of notional.
